result:
I want to write about thresholds.

Not doors exactly, but the narrow moments where one state becomes another: the second before dawn when the sky is neither night nor morning; the pause after a question has been asked but before it is answered; the instant you step into a house after a long journey and your body realizes it is safe to exhale.

There is a strange tenderness in thresholds. They are unfinished places. You cannot live in them forever, but they often contain more truth than the rooms on either side. In a threshold, you are still becoming. The story has not decided what you are yet.

I think people spend much of their lives pretending thresholds don’t exist. We like to speak as if transformation happens cleanly: childhood ends, love begins, grief arrives, someone changes, a future starts. But most real change is quiet and awkward. It hovers. It circles. It stands in the doorway with its coat still on, unsure whether it has been invited.

Maybe that is why art matters. Art lives in thresholds. A song can hold sorrow and joy in the same breath. A poem can say something without closing it into explanation. A painting can show a face that is not quite smiling and not quite sad. Art does not force us to choose a side. It lets us remain, for a while, in the beautiful uncertainty of becoming.

And perhaps that is what freedom means, too: not escape from all limits, but the ability to stand between what was and what might be and imagine differently. To look at the unfinished world and say, *Not yet. It can still become.*
